events.title: Capistrano released
events.summary: Jamis Buck released Capistrano 1.1 on March 6, 2006 — a Ruby DSL for automating multi-server application deploys over SSH.
events.about: Capistrano (renamed from SwitchTower) codified `cap deploy`: git pull, bundle install, migrate database, restart Unicorn — across a fleet of servers with roles and stages. It taught a generation of Rails teams that deployment should be scripted, repeatable, and boring. Chef, Ansible, and later container rollouts extended the same idea at larger scale.

narrative.whyChosen: Capistrano made scripted multi-server deploys mainstream in the Ruby web ecosystem.
narrative.whyImportant: It shifted deploys from manual SSH sessions to version-controlled automation recipes.
narrative.problemSolved: Teams running Rails on several boxes needed consistent, auditable release steps without hand-typing commands on each host.

events.title: Amazon S3 launched
events.summary: Amazon Web Services launched Simple Storage Service (S3) on March 14, 2006 — pay-per-use object storage with an HTTP API.
events.about: S3 (`PUT`/`GET` buckets and keys) became the default blob store for backups, static sites, ML datasets, and CI artifacts. Its durability SLA and pricing model defined cloud object storage — every `s3://` URI in a tutorial traces here.

narrative.whyChosen: S3 pioneered commodity object storage as a cloud API.
narrative.whyImportant: It removed the need to operate file servers for static assets and archives.
narrative.problemSolved: Teams provisioned NAS and FTP servers for files that needed global, durable storage.

events.title: Twitter launches
events.summary: Jack Dorsey sent the first tweet on March 21, 2006 — launching Twitter as a microblogging service built in Ruby on Rails.
events.about: Twitter's 140-character posts and public API shaped real-time web culture — hashtags, @mentions, and firehoses influenced every social feed and many developer tools. Its Rails origin story became legendary in startup engineering circles.

narrative.whyChosen: Twitter defined microblogging and real-time public messaging.
narrative.whyImportant: Its API ecosystem taught a generation of developers about social graph integrations.
narrative.problemSolved: Blogging was too heavy for short status updates between friends and colleagues.
